item.title: Jax Morning Brief — DHS Voter-Op Blocked, Oil Spikes on Iran, Anthropic IPO Pending
item.description: A federal judge halts a DHS door-to-door voter operation across nine states days before the midterms, oil surges past $113 on unconfirmed Hormuz strikes, and Anthropic's blockbuster IPO filing is still pending as of air time.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, October 23rd. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: A federal judge just blocked a Homeland Security operation that sent agents door to door asking people about their citizenship and voting history across nine states, ruling it amounts to voter intimidation less than two weeks before the midterms.

ANDREW: And in what could be the biggest test yet of investor appetite for AI valuations, Anthropic's long-awaited IPO filing was expected to land today. As of this taping, it still hasn't.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Thursday at 7,663, down about 1.2 percent. The Dow finished essentially flat, up just a couple of points, at 52,868. The Nasdaq took the hardest hit, down 2.6 percent, its worst session in months, as investors grew nervous about how much the big tech companies are spending to build out AI. The ten year Treasury yield plunged 17 basis points Thursday, the sharpest one day drop since March of 2023, before ticking back up slightly this morning to just under 5 percent as traders await more data ahead of next week's Fed decision. The thirty year fixed mortgage rate eased to 7.32 percent according to Freddie Mac, down from 7.4 the week before, but still near three year highs.

ANDREW: Let's start with the national story carrying the most weight for anyone watching next month's elections.

ANDREW: A federal judge in California granted a preliminary injunction Wednesday, stopping Homeland Security agents from going door to door asking people about their citizenship and voting history. The order covers nine states: California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin. The judge found that agents were relying on records known to be inaccurate to track people down, and that doing it this close to an election amounts to voter intimidation.

JENNY: So what actually changes on the ground because of this?

ANDREW: In those nine states, the in-person visits stop immediately. The broader effort, called Operation Protect the Vote, has already produced 113 charges across 20 states over seven weeks, including 28 green card holders arrested in California last week. The Justice Department is expected to appeal. It's also worth noting this doesn't touch a separate case — DHS says it still hopes to bring a conspiracy case against Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, though no charges have been filed there.

JENNY: Nine states and no charges yet on that second piece. This one's clearly still moving.

ANDREW: It is. The plaintiffs, who include a nurses union, Voto Latino, and two California counties, argued the timing itself was the point: agents showing up at doors in the final weeks before an election. We'll keep tracking it.

ANDREW: Let's turn to the Middle East, where the temperature is also rising.

ANDREW: Overseas, oil jumped hard Thursday. Brent crude settled at just over 113 dollars a barrel, up about 4 percent, its highest close since May. That followed claims from Iranian state media that the Revolutionary Guard struck seven vessels in the Hormuz corridor, which Iran called its largest single day toll since the war began in February. The problem is nobody independent has confirmed it. The UK's maritime monitoring group has verified only one incident, a tanker hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman that caught fire. President Trump dismissed Iran's broader claim outright, saying Tehran is manufacturing fake strikes to push oil prices higher before the midterms. Separately, the New York Times reports, citing people familiar with the planning and not yet confirmed elsewhere, that the US and Israel have drawn up a three day campaign plan against Iran's nuclear and energy sites, to launch only after the November 3rd election.

JENNY: That's a lot of smoke without much confirmed fire.

ANDREW: Exactly why we're flagging the sourcing there. What is confirmed is Trump's own language yesterday. He said, quote, something is going to happen very soon, one way or another, and that most people think it happens after the election. For context, oil was trading in the 70s before this war broke out in February. Even with this week's spike, it's still well off the war's early peak above 130 dollars a barrel.

ANDREW: One more overseas note. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy told Fox News he's ready, in his words, to freeze the front line right now, keeping roughly three quarters of Ukraine's territory, as long as the US and Europe back it with security guarantees. That came hours after Russia hit Kyiv with 21 missiles and more than 200 drones, right after last week's meeting between envoy Steve Witkoff and Putin in St. Petersburg. There's a bigger diplomatic thread attached to that too. The Kremlin says China may host a first ever three way summit between Trump, Putin, and Xi at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen next month, though Beijing says it has no information on that yet.

JENNY: That's a lot of moving pieces for one week.

ANDREW: It is, and it's complicating things back in Washington too. Republican senators including Thom Tillis, John Cornyn, and Ted Cruz have all publicly criticized the administration's sanctions waiver on Russia signed earlier this month. Some are now asking whether this week's diplomatic opening makes that waiver look justified, or more like leverage traded away too early.

JENNY: Which side is winning that argument?

ANDREW: Too soon to say. Trump's defending the waiver as necessary to keep Russia at the table, and this week's talks give him real political cover. But the criticism hasn't gone away, and it's not likely to until there's an actual deal signed.

ANDREW: Jenny, let's bring it home. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at 76 degrees and mostly sunny today, about as mild as late October gets around here.

JENNY: Today was supposed to be the day former JTA chief executive Nat Ford testified before a city council committee about the agency's finances. That's not happening. Ford, who now runs Dallas's transit system, was subpoenaed last week after a seven to one committee vote, but Councilman Rory Diamond says Ford will appear voluntarily instead, on a date they're still working out, hopefully before the holidays.

ANDREW: Why back off the subpoena if he's already compelled to show up?

JENNY: Diamond's framing it as cooperation rather than confrontation, but the underlying numbers haven't gotten any less ugly. There's a 40 million dollar deficit, roughly 200 employees let go, and a newer allegation that JTA may have inflated ridership numbers on its Skyway system to help secure federal funding. Diamond's called the whole situation, quote, an absolute living nightmare.

JENNY: Downtown, council members and developers made a fresh public push this week for a 49.65 million dollar incentive package behind a 14-story tower anchored by a full service Publix. It's part of the larger Gateway Jax project, worth about 140 million dollars total. The vote on that incentive deal is deliberately set for November 4th, the day after the Amendment 3 election, so it doesn't become a campaign issue first.

ANDREW: Smart timing, politically.

JENNY: That's one way to put it. One more local story worth flagging: the Jacksonville Housing Finance Authority is asking the city to back 100 million dollars in bonds to help first-time homebuyers get into the market.

ANDREW: How big a gap are we talking about?

JENNY: A big one. The median home price in Duval County is now somewhere around 335,000 dollars, and Jacksonville recently ranked 14th among the most financially stressful cities in the country for renters. The Authority hasn't released specifics yet on how the bond money would actually be structured or distributed, and it still needs council approval before any of it moves forward.

JENNY: Andrew, speaking of money and deadlines, what's the latest on mortgage rates?

ANDREW: Rates finally eased a bit this week. Freddie Mac's survey has the thirty year fixed at 7.32 percent, down from 7.4 the week before.

JENNY: Does a dip that small actually change anything for someone trying to buy right now?

ANDREW: Honestly, not much yet. It's still nearly a full point higher than a year ago, when rates sat at 6.19 percent. Mortgage applications fell 5.3 percent last week according to the Mortgage Bankers Association, and purchase applications are down 18 percent from a year ago. Pending home sales hit a record low. The next real catalyst is the Fed's meeting next Wednesday. Markets are now pricing in better than a 90 percent chance the Fed holds rates steady, which means Fed Chair Kevin Warsh isn't expected to hand buyers any relief soon.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, FHFA Director Bill Pulte is still weighing whether to drop the requirement that lenders pull all three credit bureau reports, plus a broader review of loan level pricing adjustments. He's promised to settle both before year end, but neither moved this week.

JENNY: So for someone who's been waiting on the sidelines, there's still no green light.

ANDREW: Not really. Fannie Mae's own forecast has rates grinding sideways in the mid sevens into next year. The one real wildcard is whether the Fed says anything unexpected next Wednesday.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for technology. What's happening with Anthropic?

JENNY: The story everyone in AI has been waiting for still hasn't actually happened. Multiple outlets, citing people familiar with the plans, say Anthropic could publicly file its IPO paperwork as soon as today. As of this taping, nothing has shown up on the SEC's public filing system.

ANDREW: What are the numbers people expect to see when it does land?

JENNY: Draft figures reviewed by the Wall Street Journal and Reuters show first half revenue around 16.3 billion dollars, but also a stunning 80 billion dollar net loss, though most of that, about 72 billion, is a non-cash accounting charge tied to convertible notes rather than money actually spent. Anthropic has told investors third quarter revenue hit nearly 17 billion, up sharply from 11.5 billion in the second quarter, and says it's now posted two straight quarters of adjusted profitability. Valuation talk has run as high as 2 trillion dollars. None of it is confirmed until the real filing lands, so take it as a draft, not a fact.

ANDREW: Worth watching closely. OpenAI already pushed its own IPO to 2027, so this would be the first real public test of how much investors trust these valuations.

JENNY: Half the AI industry's valuation story is riding on numbers nobody's technically seen yet.

ANDREW: Which is exactly why today's filing, whenever it actually lands, is going to get read line by line.

JENNY: One more from the AI world. Two Google DeepMind researchers in London resigned this week over the company's classified Pentagon AI contract and a 1.2 billion dollar cloud deal with Israel, saying they have no visibility into how their models get used militarily.

ANDREW: That's the kind of friction we're going to keep seeing as these labs sign bigger defense and government contracts.

JENNY: And in a smaller but telling move, the Chinese AI firms DeepSeek and MiniMax both completed registration under Beijing's new AI export rules this week. It suggests China is routing its response to Washington's procurement ban through its own regulations rather than direct retaliation.

ANDREW: A quieter path, but still one more sign of how fast AI policy is becoming a two way street between Washington and Beijing.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: next Wednesday's Fed decision. Markets are pricing in better than a 90 percent chance of a hold, so the real story will be what Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says afterward about December. Any hint of a shift there would move mortgage rates and markets fast.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you Monday.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Hormuz Tensions Spike, Putin Talks Advance, Anthropic Nears IPO Filing
item.description: Iran claims its largest single-day toll of tanker strikes near the Strait of Hormuz, even as a U.S. envoy meets Putin and a hostage comes home. Plus: JTA's surprise reversal, mortgage rates stuck near 7.4 percent, and Anthropic's imminent IPO filing.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, October 22nd. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Iran claims its forces struck seven vessels overnight near the Strait of Hormuz — what could be the largest single-day toll since that war began back in February. And in the same twenty-four hours, a U.S. envoy sat down with Vladimir Putin for three hours, and Russia released an American held for more than four years.

ANDREW: And here in the world of artificial intelligence, Anthropic may file for what could be the biggest IPO of the year as early as tomorrow. We'll get into the eye-popping numbers in that draft prospectus.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,757, up six-tenths of a percent. The Dow closed at 52,856, up seven-tenths of a percent — a one-month high. The Nasdaq climbed to 26,703, up one-point-one percent. That's three straight days of gains, powered by strong earnings — SpaceX jumped nearly eight percent on its AI business — as Wall Street heads into the heart of Big Tech earnings season. The ten-year Treasury yield is holding around five-point-one percent, steady ahead of next week's Fed meeting. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at seven-point-four percent, according to both Freddie Mac and Mortgage News Daily. And oil remains elevated near 110 dollars a barrel on Strait of Hormuz tension — which brings us to our lead story.

ANDREW: Let's start in the Middle East and Moscow, because there's a lot moving at once. Iran's state media says its forces struck seven vessels overnight — four tankers it accuses of illegal ship-to-ship transfers, plus three more it says hit mines near the strait. Iran is calling it the biggest single-day tally of the war.

JENNY: Seven vessels in one night — is that actually confirmed, or is that just what Iran is saying?

ANDREW: Good question, and it matters. That count comes from Iranian state media only — no independent maritime tracker has confirmed vessel names, flags, or casualties, and the U.S. military has previously attributed similar damage to missiles and drones rather than mines. Brent crude did spike above 110 dollars intraday on the claims before settling back near 108. Separately, the New York Times is reporting that the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for a roughly three-day campaign against Iranian nuclear and energy sites — but only after the November 3rd midterms. That's a single Times report, not yet confirmed elsewhere, and Trump reportedly postponed a strike earlier this month at the last minute.

JENNY: So nothing imminent, but the planning is real.

ANDREW: That's the read right now. Meanwhile, there's a more hopeful thread on Russia. Special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg for about three hours yesterday, and Putin agreed in principle to restart three-way peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S., tentatively around November 10th, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Russia also released American Stephen Hubbard, who'd been detained more than four years. Zelenskyy has signaled he's open to freezing the front line as a first step.

JENNY: That's a real de-escalation, at least on paper. Does it clash at all with the sanctions fight we've been following?

ANDREW: It actually makes that fight more awkward for the White House. Trump's waiver on Russia sanctions, signed back on the 16th, is drawing a wider bipartisan backlash. Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible." Senator Cornyn said the late Senator Lindsey Graham, whose sanctions law this waives, "would be appalled." Trump is defending the move on Truth Social, saying he's negotiating peace and doesn't want to drive Russia away from the table. With actual peace talks now back on the calendar, Trump's argument gets a little more ammunition — but so does the criticism that he's trading leverage for a photo op.

ANDREW: One more item from Washington. CBS News is reporting that hundreds of DHS agents have been reassigned to in-person home visits in at least six states — California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin — asking residents directly about their citizenship and voting history. It's part of the same "Operation Protect the Vote" sweep that's already brought charges against 113 people in 20 states, including 28 green-card holders arrested in California this week. Voting-rights groups have sued over the home visits, and a 23-year veteran of the agency told CBS he's never seen anything like it. It's worth noting this runs on a parallel track to the ongoing investigation into Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, where DHS says it has a "strong case" but still hasn't filed charges.

JENNY: All two weeks before the midterms.

ANDREW: Exactly the timing everyone's watching. One more quick item: Trump announced an 8 billion dollar relief program for farmers this week, a one-time payment to offset diesel costs this harvest season, funded through the Commodity Credit Corporation. Diesel's been running around six-dollars-thirty a gallon nationally, close to a record, partly because of the same Middle East supply jitters we just talked about.

JENNY: So the Hormuz tension is already showing up on American farms.

ANDREW: That's the connective tissue here — oil disruption overseas turning into a federal bailout at home. Jenny, what's happening at home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 77 and mostly sunny skies today — though if you're headed to the beach, there's a real rip current risk from a nor'easter moving in this weekend.

JENNY: The biggest local story is actually a non-event. City Council subpoenaed former JTA CEO Nat Ford — he now runs Dallas's transit agency — to testify tomorrow about the agency's financial collapse. But News4Jax is reporting that appearance isn't happening. Councilman Rory Diamond, who pushed for the subpoena, now says he's hoping to get Ford on the record sometime before the holidays instead.

ANDREW: Didn't the council just vote to subpoena him this week? That's a quick reversal.

JENNY: It is — the committee voted seven-to-one on Tuesday to compel him, and now Ford's team says he'll appear voluntarily rather than show up under subpoena. Diamond, for what it's worth, called JTA "an absolute living nightmare" — citing a 40 million dollar deficit, roughly 200 employees let go, and a new allegation that JTA may have inflated its Skyway ridership numbers to qualify for federal funding. A second subpoena, covering internal communications between interim CEO Cleveland Ferguson, Ford, and Mayor Deegan's office, is still due October 30th.

JENNY: Separately, the Jacksonville Housing Finance Authority is asking the city to back 100 million dollars in bonds to help first-time homebuyers, according to Action News Jax. That comes as the median single-family home price in Duval County has climbed to around 335,000 dollars, and one recent ranking put Jacksonville 14th among the most financially stressful U.S. cities for renters.

ANDREW: A hundred million is a real commitment. Any sense of how far that stretches?

JENNY: Not yet specified — it still needs council approval — but it's a signal city leaders see affordability as the pressing issue right now. And quickly, two other things we're tracking: the incentive vote for that downtown Publix-anchored tower is still on hold until after the Amendment 3 election on November 3rd, and JEA says further rate increases are now under discussion on top of the hike that already took effect this month. Andrew, speaking of housing costs, what's happening on the mortgage side?

ANDREW: It's a similar story nationally — rates stuck, and buyers pulling back. The 30-year fixed is holding right around seven-point-four percent. That number comes from both Freddie Mac's weekly survey and Mortgage News Daily's daily index, which is a solid, independently-confirmed anchor. It's essentially unchanged from last week, but still near three-year highs.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for someone trying to buy right now?

ANDREW: It means a lot of people are sitting it out. The Mortgage Bankers Association says applications fell five-point-three percent last week, with purchase applications down seven percent — eighteen percent below where they were a year ago. Pending home sales nationally hit a record low, down seven-point-three percent. Builder confidence is at its weakest October reading since 2012. And Fannie Mae's latest forecast doesn't expect real relief — they're projecting rates averaging around seven-point-four percent through the rest of this year and seven-point-five percent across all of 2027.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, FHFA Director Bill Pulte is exploring ending the requirement that lenders pull credit reports from all three bureaus for loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — moving to just one or two reports instead, which he's framing as a cost-saving move for borrowers. He's also said FHFA will decide on broader pricing adjustments before year end.

JENNY: Worth watching if that actually brings costs down for buyers.

ANDREW: It could shave a little off closing costs, though it won't move the rate itself. The bigger driver next week is the Fed's tone, not the decision — markets already expect them to hold. Jenny, what's the latest in tech?

JENNY: The headline is one that hasn't quite happened yet, but it's close. Anthropic is reportedly planning to publicly file for an IPO as early as tomorrow — which would make it the biggest AI listing of the year, especially since OpenAI has pushed its own IPO to 2027.

ANDREW: What are the numbers looking like, if the draft prospectus holds up?

JENNY: This is where it gets interesting. The Wall Street Journal reviewed a draft showing first-half 2026 revenue of 16.3 billion dollars — up from just 1.1 billion a year earlier. But it also shows a net loss of roughly 80.7 billion dollars.

ANDREW: Wait, an 80 billion dollar loss on 16 billion in revenue? That doesn't sound like a company that's ready to go public.

JENNY: It's less alarming than it sounds — about 72 billion of that loss is a non-cash accounting charge tied to how convertible bonds get valued, not money actually going out the door. Anthropic has separately told investors its third-quarter revenue hit 16.8 billion dollars, up from 11.5 billion in the second quarter, and that it's now posted adjusted profitability for two straight quarters with positive cash flow. Nothing's official until the filing actually lands — EDGAR doesn't show it yet as of this morning — but if it comes tomorrow as expected, it'll be a real test of investor appetite for AI valuations.

JENNY: There's also a smaller, more human story out of Google this week. Two DeepMind researchers in London resigned, citing ethical concerns over the company's AI contracts with the U.S. and Israeli militaries — part of a broader Pentagon push to bring AI companies into classified defense networks. It's a reminder that not everyone inside these labs is comfortable with where the technology is heading, even as the business side races toward IPOs and bigger government deals.

ANDREW: Good context after the money talk.

JENNY: One more from the AI world. The Department of Homeland Security has confirmed an order banning federal civilian agencies from buying or using China's DeepSeek AI models — the Pentagon is exempt. China's government has called it discriminatory and says it will take "all necessary measures" to protect its companies, though nothing concrete yet.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch by Friday: whether Anthropic's IPO filing actually lands. If it does, watch which revenue and loss figures show up — the numbers circulating this week have varied wildly between leaked drafts, and the real filing will settle which set was closer to the truth. It'll also be the first hard test of how public markets price a company burning cash on this scale while still calling itself profitable on paper.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Johnson's Russia Warning, Anthropic's Leaked Revenue, Rates Hold
item.description: Speaker Johnson confirms he warned the White House on the Russia sanctions waiver. Anthropic's leaked IPO filing reveals explosive revenue and a confusing loss. Jacksonville's JTA saga deepens, and mortgage rates hold in the mid sevens.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, October 21st. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: House Speaker Mike Johnson just confirmed, on the record, that he personally warned the White House about quote unintended consequences from the president's decision to waive sanctions on Russia. That's the sitting Speaker publicly breaking with his own party's strategy.

ANDREW: And a leaked draft of Anthropic's IPO paperwork shows the AI company brought in more than sixteen billion dollars in revenue in the first half of this year alone. There's a catch to that number, and we'll get into it.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand seven hundred twelve, up about a quarter of a percent. The Dow closed at fifty two thousand four hundred ninety six, up roughly five hundred thirty points, or just over one percent, its best day in weeks on strong earnings. The Nasdaq closed at twenty six thousand four hundred twenty five, essentially flat, down two hundredths of a percent, as AI stocks pulled in the other direction. The ten year Treasury yield is holding around five point one two percent. And the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is sitting in the mid sevens — Freddie Mac's weekly survey has it at seven point four percent, unchanged from last week. We'll dig into what that means a little later in the show.

ANDREW: Let's start with Washington, because the biggest story right now is about trust inside the president's own party. Last week, President Trump signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs on Russia under the law that's informally known as the Lindsey Graham Russia and Iran sanctions act. The waiver has no expiration date. Over the weekend, Speaker Johnson went on Fox News and said, in his own words, that he told the White House directly there could be unintended consequences.

JENNY: Wait, the Speaker said this on television, not through an aide or a leaked memo?

ANDREW: Correct, on camera, to Larry Kudlow. That's a significant upgrade from earlier reporting that had this as a secondhand account. Senator Thom Tillis called the waiver, quote, beyond irresponsible. Representatives Michael McCaul and Don Bacon also criticized it, though Representative Thomas Massie has defended the president's move. The White House's reasoning is that keeping the waiver in place keeps Russia at the negotiating table and helps hold down fuel prices heading into the midterms.

ANDREW: Speaking of fuel prices, the Strait of Hormuz situation remains unresolved. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed today that mines struck three tankers, including a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels that allegedly caught fire. Independent maritime trackers say they can't confirm the vessel names or locations, so for now, treat that as an Iranian state media claim, not a confirmed incident. Brent crude is trading near a hundred and ten dollars a barrel, the highest level in about five months. Qatar has floated a seven day plan to help calm the strait, and Iran's foreign minister says Qatar is bringing, quote, new ideas to the table, but the US hasn't signed on yet. The president continues to say there will be no US strikes before the November third midterms.

JENNY: So where does that leave the Federal Reserve, with oil prices this unsettled?

ANDREW: That's the backdrop heading into the Fed's October twenty eighth meeting. Prediction markets now put the odds of a hold at around eighty five to eighty eight percent, with a possible hike pushed to December. That's partly because September's jobs report badly missed expectations — just twenty nine thousand jobs added against a forecast of eighty four thousand, and unemployment ticked up to four point two percent. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has declined to tip his hand on an October move, which the market is reading as a green light for a pause.

ANDREW: One more item from the national desk. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said publicly this week that investigators have what he called a strong case against Representative Ilhan Omar and plan to bring it before a grand jury, in the ongoing investigation into whether she misstated her birth year on naturalization paperwork decades ago. No charges have been filed as of this morning, and her attorneys are still pressing the Justice Department over property seized during an earlier search. Her reelection bid is on the ballot November third.

ANDREW: Separately, the Justice Department says it's now charged twenty eight green card holders in California with illegally voting, part of a seven week sweep it's calling Operation Protect the Vote that now covers a hundred and thirteen people across twenty states. It's drawing extra attention because of its timing, two weeks before the midterms, and its thematic overlap with the Omar case.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening back home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a sunny, breezy day today — high near seventy eight, low around fifty seven, with next to no chance of rain. A genuinely pleasant fall day.

JENNY: The City Council has escalated its fight to get answers out of JTA, the transit authority facing a thirty nine million dollar budget shortfall. The Council has now subpoenaed former JTA CEO Nat Ford — who's since moved on to run Dallas's transit agency — to testify before the Finance Committee this Friday, October twenty third, about the agency's financial collapse.

ANDREW: Didn't the city also subpoena Mayor Deegan directly for records?

JENNY: It did. That deadline was Monday, and her office said someone from the general counsel's office would deliver the records by mail, but there's no independent confirmation yet that it actually happened. A second, broader subpoena covering interim JTA CEO Cleveland Ferguson, Ford, and the mayor's own communications is due by October thirtieth. This is a story we'll keep following closely.

JENNY: Downtown, the Publix tower planned for Pearl Square is still on hold. The roughly fifty million dollar incentive package for that hundred forty million dollar project has been pushed to a November fourth Finance Committee vote, deliberately scheduled after next week's Amendment Three election, with Council President Nick Howland saying he wants to see those results first.

JENNY: And JEA customers are feeling it in their bills. Electric, water, and sewer rates went up this month, adding roughly eight dollars to a typical monthly bill, as the utility works through a budget shortfall of its own, this one topping a hundred million dollars. Some council members are now discussing pulling about two million dollars from city reserves to help residents who are struggling to keep up.

JENNY: And over at the stadium, the Jaguars' one point four billion dollar Stadium of the Future renovation remains on schedule. The team is playing a reduced capacity season here in Jacksonville, around forty five thousand seats, before shifting home games to Orlando next season while construction wraps up ahead of twenty twenty eight.

ANDREW: That's a long runway for a stadium bet that size.

JENNY: Andrew, what's the latest on the mortgage side?

ANDREW: Rates were basically flat this week, and that flatness is itself the story. Freddie Mac's benchmark weekly survey puts the thirty year fixed at seven point four percent, unchanged from a week ago. Day to day lender surveys are bouncing around a bit more, anywhere from the high sevens to the low sevens depending on the source, but the broad picture is the same: mortgage rates are stuck in a narrow mid-seven percent band.

JENNY: Does that track with what the Fed is doing, or is something else driving it?

ANDREW: It's mostly something else. Mortgage rates move with the ten year Treasury yield and mortgage bond pricing more than they move with the Fed meeting calendar directly, and that yield has been stuck near five point one percent on lingering inflation uncertainty, not anticipation of next week's decision. Warsh staying quiet on October just reinforces that nothing is likely to shift until there's more clarity on where inflation is actually heading.

ANDREW: The volume numbers tell the real story about demand. The Mortgage Bankers Association says applications fell two point seven percent in the most recent week, with purchase applications down four percent and now running about sixteen percent below year ago levels. Adjustable rate mortgages have climbed to ten and a half percent of applications, the highest share in about a year, as some buyers look for any way to lower their monthly payment. Refinancing is down fifty six percent from a year ago, even though refinances now make up nearly thirty eight percent of all applications, a sign of just how far purchase lending has pulled back.

ANDREW: Fannie Mae, meanwhile, cut its own forecast for next year's mortgage originations by eighteen percent, citing rates that are staying higher for longer and refinancing demand that just isn't showing up. And at the regulatory level, FHFA Director Bill Pulte is reportedly reviewing whether to drop the requirement that lenders pull all three credit bureau reports on every loan, with a decision possibly coming by year end — that one's still in the consideration stage, not a final rule.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's the latest out of AI this week?

JENNY: The headline is Anthropic's IPO paperwork. There's still no public filing on the SEC's system as of this morning, but the Wall Street Journal reviewed a draft prospectus and reported some eye-popping numbers: sixteen point three billion dollars in revenue in just the first half of this year, up from one point one billion a year earlier.

ANDREW: Wait, sixteen billion in six months? What's the catch you mentioned at the top of the show?

JENNY: The same draft shows a net loss of about eighty point seven billion dollars, which sounds alarming until you learn that roughly seventy two billion of that is non-cash accounting charges tied to how certain financial instruments and funding rounds get valued on paper, not actual cash burned running the business. The draft also shows compute commitments topping six hundred billion dollars, and two customers accounting for roughly a fifth of all first-half revenue. Worth flagging, these figures come from one outlet's review of a leaked document, so treat the exact numbers as provisional until the company files publicly. Analysts think that public filing needs to land in the next few days to keep a November ninth roadshow on track.

JENNY: Separately, China's government has publicly pushed back against the new Department of Homeland Security order banning DeepSeek technology from federal civilian agencies, warning of possible retaliatory measures. That order, tied to a two thousand eighteen supply chain security law, doesn't touch the Pentagon or private sector use, but it's become a flashpoint because DeepSeek's cheap models have been undercutting pricing across the industry.

ANDREW: That IPO number also lands right after Anthropic's other big headline from last week, a pledge to commit five percent of its equity to a new public benefit fund, which prompted Elon Musk to counter with a promise to give a share of SpaceX to every American child starting in twenty twenty seven. Neither company has spelled out exactly how either pledge actually gets distributed yet.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: the Federal Reserve's meeting next Wednesday, October twenty eighth. Prediction markets are leaning toward a hold, with odds near eighty five percent, but that weak September jobs report has kept December hike odds alive too. Watch Fed Chair Warsh's language after the meeting for any signal on where rates go next — that's what will actually move mortgage rates from here, not the October decision itself.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
